nameStory: The name 'periwinkle' comes from the Latin 'pervinca,' meaning 'to bind around' or 'entwine,' referring to how this plant's trailing stems weave together to form dense mats. 'Lesser' distinguishes it from its larger cousin, greater periwinkle, though this smaller version is actually more common in New England gardens.
description: Lesser periwinkle is a low-growing, evergreen groundcover that spreads by trailing stems to form dense carpets. It typically stays under 6 inches tall but can spread several feet wide, creating thick mats of glossy green leaves. In spring, it produces cheerful purple-blue flowers that peek up above the foliage like little stars.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five flat, blue-purple petals form pinwheel-shaped flowers about an inch across, blooming in spring. Each petal has a slightly squared-off tip, and the flowers sit on short stems above the leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite pairs of glossy, dark green leaves feel thick and leathery to the touch. Each leaf is oval-shaped, about 1-2 inches long, with smooth edges and a prominent central vein.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Trailing stems root at the nodes as they creep along the ground, forming dense, evergreen mats. The stems feel somewhat woody and can extend 1-2 feet in all directions from the original plant.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Long, flexible runners spread horizontally across the ground, rooting where they touch soil. Break a stem and you'll see a milky white sap that's characteristic of the dogbane family.

habitat: Lesser periwinkle thrives in shaded to partially shaded areas with moist, well-drained soil, commonly found in gardens, parks, and naturalized areas throughout New England. It often escapes cultivation to form colonies under trees, along woodland edges, and in shaded urban areas. You'll frequently spot it growing alongside other shade-loving groundcovers like pachysandra in residential landscapes.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming season with abundant purple-blue flowers appearing from April through May. This is the best time to spot periwinkle, as the colorful blooms make it stand out against the dark green foliage.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but the glossy green leaves remain prominent, forming dense evergreen mats. Occasionally produces scattered blooms throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Foliage stays green and healthy-looking through autumn, maintaining its groundcover role while many other plants are dying back or changing color.
seasonality.winter: Leaves persist through winter, staying green under snow cover. The evergreen foliage makes it easily identifiable even in the coldest months when most other groundcovers have died back.

funFact: Lesser periwinkle contains the same alkaloids used to make important cancer-fighting drugs, including vincristine and vinblastine, which are used to treat childhood leukemia and other cancers – making this humble garden groundcover a genuine lifesaver.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with greater periwinkle, but lesser periwinkle has smaller leaves (under 2 inches vs. over 2 inches) and shorter stems that hug the ground more closely. Remember: 'lesser' means smaller leaves and lower growth habit.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'myrtle' in some parts of the United States, lesser periwinkle is completely unrelated to true myrtles and shouldn't be confused with them. This naming confusion arose simply because both plants are used as evergreen groundcovers in landscaping.
compareHints: Lesser periwinkle is much more common in New England than greater periwinkle (Vinca major), which has noticeably larger leaves (over 2 inches long) and more upright growth reaching 8-12 inches tall. Greater periwinkle also has slightly larger flowers and is less cold-hardy, making it less suitable for New England's harsh winters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Greater periwinkle is much larger than lesser periwinkle in every way - bigger leaves, bigger flowers, and more aggressive spreading habit.
